summary:
Pomeranian Voivodeship stands under Poland's national framework, and the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in that framework is detention. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention reported that a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. The Border Guard refused to move or release her despite her identification as a woman and her warning that stopping the medication would harm her; the Border Guard Commander ordered her release only after the legal-aid organisation intervened, citing Polish law, court rulings and international standards, on the ground that continued detention there posed a serious health risk. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months while she was held. The case also recorded her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may face both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene against that pattern. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans woman hormone replacement therapy while she was imprisoned, despite hormones having been prescribed to her for almost two years, and awarded EUR 8,000 in damages. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status.

Protection on gender-identity grounds is not yet in force. There is no hate-crime protection covering sexual orientation or gender identity; a March 2025 amendment bill was referred to the Constitutional Tribunal, with hearings held in July and September 2025. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation, and a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, with a second bill following in late October 2024. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024, and the status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.
tangentialFactors:
The anti-LGBT municipal-resolution wave reached more than 80 municipalities and four voivodeship-level declarations as of March 2020, concentrated in the eastern and south-eastern parts of Poland. Pomeranian Voivodeship does not appear in that concentration, but the absence of local findings here indicates thinner documentation rather than established safety: the national rules on detention, hate-crime coverage and legal gender recognition apply regardless of municipal declarations.

The two documented trans-specific incidents in the national record are both custody cases rather than street-level incidents, which shifts the practical exposure for a visitor from public-order policing toward what happens after a detention or a border-control encounter. The Canadian advisory's list of harassment motives places sexual orientation next to foreigner status, so a trans visitor who is also visibly foreign may be read through both categories at once.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition in Poland remains court-based and medically gatekept, requiring a judicial proceeding and expert assessment rather than an administrative application.

Same-sex couples have no partnership framework: the September 2024 European Court of Human Rights ruling characterised the absence of recognition as an illegal vacuum contrary to couples' rights and called for a recognition framework to be established. Marriage certificates obtained abroad were blocked from recognition under a directive issued by Justice Minister Ziobro until Justice Minister Bodnar revoked it in June 2024.

The Prosecutor General has established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement on hate incidents, and a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation has been announced by Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek.

Trans people held in Polish prisons have a Convention remedy against denial of hormone replacement therapy following the 11 July 2024 judgment, but obtaining the medication in practice has required litigation rather than an internal complaint process.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the hate-speech and Penal Code amendment bills at the time of travel is unresolved in this record; the bills were before the Constitutional Tribunal with hearings in July and September 2025, and no sourced outcome is available here.

No source in this inventory identifies which guarded centre for male foreign nationals serves Pomeranian Voivodeship, or whether any trans detainee has been held in a facility within the voivodeship. The March 2024 case is documented at national level without a named location.

Whether Pomeranian Voivodeship or any municipality within it adopted an anti-LGBT declaration in the 2019–2020 wave is not sourced here; the inventory places the wave in the eastern and south-eastern parts of the country without listing individual units.

Enforcement of the EUR 8,000 award and any subsequent change to Polish prison practice on hormone therapy following the European Court of Human Rights judgment are not sourced.
